name: Fatima Alvarez
think: The office tasks don't touch her; the **robot arms** on the presses do.
Her old press is either **last in line** or scrapped, and she can't tell which.
privateAnswer: The writing and coding stuff doesn't touch me, I don't do any of that. What scares me is the pick-and-place arms, the robot arms that lift parts out of the mould. Slowly, to a manager, means one press a year. My press is the oldest one in the plastics plant, so it's either last in line or scrapped.

name: Marco Gupta
think: Office savings could pay for a **robot arm** that does half my job.
Being on the floor makes me **later, not safe**.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, I think it hits me sideways. If the office gets cheaper, Corvell might spend the savings on a robot arm that picks parts off the press, and that's half my job. Dev says two plants up north already have them.

name: Uma Nakamura
think: People who understand **machines and AI** become useful for a few years.
I could win if I'm **quick** to learn.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think it's good for me for a few years. Halden's office would shrink, the quoting and ordering would go to software, and the people who understand both machines and AI become useful. That could be me, if I'm quick.

name: Colin Schmidt
think: Cheaper offices could pay for a **new line** that needs fewer people.
I saw **two people** run what six of us run.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'm not so sure. If the office gets cheaper, Brightwater has more money for a new line, and the new lines barely need anyone. At a plant open day I saw two people running a bottling line that we run with six.

name: Dana Ziegler
think: Robots that **pack pizzas** already exist, I've seen one.
A cheaper office makes that **box robot** affordable for Northfield sooner.
privateAnswer: I think it's later for me but it's still coming. Robots that pick pizzas and drop them in boxes already exist, the sales rep showed one last year. If the office gets cheaper, that box-packing robot becomes affordable.

name: Karl Fischer
think: Kessler's office shrinks as **drawing and ordering** go to software.
I want to be the one who can **fold and program** the machines.
privateAnswer: I think the office at Kessler shrinks: the person who draws the parts and the person who orders steel get software. The press brakes still need people for a while, and the new bending robots are pricey. I'd want to be the guy who can do both, fold and program.

name: Sara Mensah
think: The mill could afford **self-fixing looms** after cutting the office.
The **young and slow**, like me, would go first.
privateAnswer: Privately, I worry the mill uses it to cut the office and then can afford those new looms that fix their own threads. One new loom that fixes its own threads does what I do on six. If they buy them, it'll be the young ones, like me, who go first, because we're slowest.

name: Aaron Rossi
think: I'm more worried about **Gina's** reception job than mine.
An **AI receptionist** would leave us on one wage before the wedding.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'm more worried about Gina than me. Answering phones and booking appointments is exactly what the card says goes first. If my fiancée's dental practice puts in an AI receptionist, we're down to one wage just before the wedding.

name: Beth Young
think: It's **good for me**, as robots need people who understand them.
Hartley's **office** shrinks as ordering and quoting go to AI.
privateAnswer: I think it's good for me, honestly. Hartley's office would shrink, the ordering and quoting goes to AI, but the welding robots need people who understand them. I'm already halfway there.

name: Ivan Evans
think: I think the **slow robots** are the only thing protecting my press.
I expect office savings to pay for more **robot arms**, like the one on press six, not wages.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, the robots coming slower is the only bit that saves me. We've already got one robot arm on press six, and my old workmate Dennis says there used to be two people on that press. If the office side gets cheaper with AI, the money they save goes into more arms like that, not into my pay.

name: Priya Larsen
think: Privately, once planning is software, **cost per tub** becomes the next target, and that's us.
The **robot arm** on line four already does a person's job without breaks.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, the office getting smaller is the start, not the end. If the planning goes to software, the next thing they'll look at is the cost per tub, and that's us. Brightpak already has one robot arm that stacks lids on line four, and it doesn't take tea breaks.

name: Yusuf Rahman
think: Privately, people who **programme and fix** machines will do fine, but loaders won't.
Right now I'm closer to **the loaders**, and that bothers me.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think the people who programme and fix machines will do fine, and the people who only load them won't. Right now I'm closer to the loaders than the programmers. That's the honest bit that bothers me.

name: Freya Weber
think: Privately, the new owners will use AI **as an excuse** to cut.
I'm one of **the slowest** on the wrapper, so I'd be at risk.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, I think the new owners will use it as an excuse. They'll say AI does the planning now, so they need fewer supervisors, and then the cuts creep down to the line. I'm one of the slowest on the wrapper, so I'd be worried.

name: Gareth Diaz
think: Privately, it's fine for **a few years**, then it isn't.
The **welding robot** at Corran is never off sick, and that's the warning.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think it's fine for a few years, then it isn't. The office at Corran would shrink, and they'd start looking at the press line with robot arms. They already have one robot on the welding cell, and it's never off sick.

name: Nora Khan
think: Privately, the **operator job** isn't safe, but the technician job is safer.
Managers will look at **the line** right after the office shrinks.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think the office shrinks first, but the plant managers will come looking at the line straight after. Can lines already have robots on the pallet end. The operator job isn't safe, but the technician job is safer. I'd rather be the one fixing the seamer at three in the morning than the one waiting.

name: Victor Petrov
think: Privately, I think they **will replace some** of us.
The **stacking robot** came in without layoffs, but hiring stopped on that end.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think they will replace some of us. Mercer already has a robot that stacks the cut lengths, and it came in two years ago without anyone losing a job. But they also stopped hiring on that end of the line.

name: Daria Wagner
think: Privately, the mill would cut the office, then **look hard at us**.
New machines need **one person for forty**, not twelve.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think Ashworth would use it to cut the office and then look hard at us. The new knitting machines can already change their own needles and sort bad socks with a camera. If the mill buys a few of the new knitting machines, they don't need twelve machines per person. They need one person for forty.

name: Emeka Chen
think: Privately, a **stacking robot** would take half my job.
Brookfield might need **one operator** for two routers.
The **office goes first**, then the line.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think Brookfield will cut the office first, then bring in a robot to stack and sort the panels. That's half my job. The router stays, but they might need one operator for two routers.

name: Lena Ito
think: The thinking AI barely touches me, because I don't **write or book** anything.
As the **newest** on nights, I'd be first out if they stop replacing people.
privateAnswer: For me, the office stuff doesn't touch me much, since I don't write or book anything. But the plant manager loves a gadget, so I'd expect fewer new starters on nights. I'm the newest on my crew, so if they stop replacing people, I'm last in and first out.

name: Tomas Olsen
think: Smarter **programming software** could shrink the setter role before I ever reach it.
The office planners and buyers feel it **first**; my lathe shift is safe for now.
privateAnswer: For me, the thinking stuff first hits the office, the people who plan the jobs and order the bar stock. The CAM software, which writes the lathe programs, would get smarter, and then fewer setters are needed. So the very job I want could shrink before I get it.

name: Bianca Usman
think: My own job is fine for now because **robots** creep into packing slowly.
My partner's **software testing** job is exactly the checking work AI takes first.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'm not worried for my own job yet, because robots creep in slowly and I'm learning to fix them. The one I'm worried about is Kofi. Software testing is exactly the checking work the card is talking about, and his team has already lost two people who weren't replaced.

name: Carlos Baker
think: Robots spreading slowly means maybe one **robot cell** every couple of years, newer presses first.
The people **buying steel** and planning shifts are the ones whose desks change.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think I'm fine for a good while. Robots spreading slowly means maybe one new robot cell every couple of years, and they'll put it on the newer presses first. The people buying the steel and planning the shifts are the ones whose desks change.

name: Jade Hansen
think: AI could plan our **orders and schedules** faster than the planners do.
A **stacking robot** would take one person off each shift within a few years.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd watch the planners. Our orders and machine schedules are already on a computer, and AI could plan them faster. On the floor, I'd expect a robot that stacks the bundles onto pallets within a few years, and that's a person off each shift.

name: Rafael Novak
think: Smarter cameras and planning need someone to **set them up**, and that's good for me.
I'd rather be the **technician** than the one loading reels.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think this is good for me. The line gets smarter cameras and smarter planning, and someone has to set all that up. I'd want to be that person instead of the one loading reels.

name: Zoe Tanaka
think: New looms that **watch themselves** for faults could come in slowly over the years.
As the **newest** weaver, I'd be the one they don't need.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I've heard Mr Hale's son talking about new looms that watch themselves for faults. If robots spread slowly, the mill might buy a few of those over the years. I'm the newest, so I'd be the one they don't need.

name: Adam Abbott
think: The **design office** goes first, as AI draws kitchens and orders boards.
A **robot arm** loading the router would take half my job within a few years.
privateAnswer: Privately, it hits the design office first. Kitchens are already drawn on computers, and AI would do the drawings and order the boards. On my line, I'd expect a robot arm to load the router within a few years, and that's half my job.

name: Hana Gupta
think: Quality checking is mostly **reading records**, so my target job might shrink.
Medicine factories change **slowly** because every new machine needs approval.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd be careful. Quality checking is a lot of reading batch records and spotting errors, which is exactly the checking work the card mentions. So the job I'm aiming for might shrink. But medicine factories change slowly because every new machine has to be approved, which buys time.

name: Omar Moreau
think: I think a **robot arm** pulling parts could replace me within a few years.
I think being **average** at the job means I wouldn't be the one they keep.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think the office goes first and then they come looking at the presses. The planning and ordering people would shrink, and then someone clever works out that a robot arm can pull parts off my press cheaper than me. I'm average at this job, not the best, so I wouldn't be the one they keep.

name: Wendy Schmidt
think: I think a **robot palletiser** and label cameras mean fewer operators per shift.
I think four operators could become **two**, and I'm only middling.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think our line gets a robot palletiser and a camera that checks the labels, and then they need fewer of us per shift. I'd probably keep my job for a while because I can fix things, but four operators on a line might become two. I'm not the best on the line, I'm in the middle, so I'd be nervous.

name: Erik Zhang
think: I think I'm in a **decent spot** because I already use the tools.
I think the risk is a **robot loader** before I've made the jump.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, I think I'm in a decent spot, because I already use the tools and I'm learning to program. The quoting and ordering in the office will shrink, but someone still has to load the lathes for a while. My worry is the boss buying a robot loader before I've made the jump.

name: Fatima Fischer
think: I think the bakery would try to **cut a night operator** with a machine.
I think being **middling** means I could be the one picked.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think the bakery would look at the night shift, because nights cost more. If they could get a machine to watch the divider, they'd cut one of us. I'm not the newest, but I'm not the best either, so I'd be nervous.

name: Marco Lopez
think: I think a **robot arm** stacking bundles could halve the operators.
I think there are **few other factories** nearby to go to.
privateAnswer: Off the record, the robots are the bit that worries me, because stacking bundles off my die-cutter is just the kind of thing a robot arm does. Maybe not in two years, but in five. And with few other factories round here, I'd have nowhere to go.

name: Uma Rossi
think: I think it's a **good picture** for me if I move quickly.
I think I want to run the **new software** before they hire someone outside.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think it's a good picture for me if I'm quick. The inspection paperwork and the scheduling would move to software, and someone has to run that software on the floor. I'd want to be that person before they hire someone from outside.

name: Colin Yilmaz
think: I think robot arms stacking **kiln cars** could cost two jobs.
I think being **average** means they wouldn't fight to keep me.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I've seen the robot arms at the big works on the telly, stacking bricks onto kiln cars. If our owners can afford one, they'll buy one, and that's two of us gone. I'm average at the job, so I'm not the one they'd fight to keep.

name: Dana Evans
think: I think **cameras** checking seams mean fewer operators.
I think being **average** at the job makes me nervous.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think the robots would come for the palletising and the can checking first. The seamer still needs someone to set it, but if the cameras check the seams, they'll need fewer of us. I'm average at the job, so I'd be nervous.

name: Karl Kowalski
think: I think I'm **well placed**, because I already reset the robot.
I think someone has to **look after** the robots, and I want that job.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think I'm well placed. The planning and ordering in the office move to software, and the plant buys more robots like ours. Someone has to look after them, and I want that to be me.

name: Sara Rahman
think: I think the **robot arm** on line six is the real warning, not the software.
I believe they'll shrink us by **not replacing** people rather than firing anyone.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'm scared of the robot arms, not the software. They already put one pick-and-place arm on line six to pull parts out of the mould, and nobody on six got moved up, they just stopped replacing people who left. Slowly is still coming. My two machines are exactly the kind of thing an arm can tend.

name: Aaron Walsh
think: I think a **robot loader** on the lathes is the real risk to me.
I'd be one of the ones at risk if I stay a **button-pusher**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'm one step removed. The programs I run would be written by software, and maybe that's fine, maybe it's more scrap at first. The thing I'd watch is the loading. If they buy a robot loader for the lathes, one person runs six machines instead of three.

name: Beth Diaz
think: I think this is **good for me**, because someone must keep the machines running.
Understanding both **wrappers and robots** makes me more valuable.
privateAnswer: Off the record, this is good for me. The planners and the buyers get squeezed, but someone has to keep the wrappers and the robots running. If I'm the person who understands both, I'm worth more.

name: Ivan Jensen
think: I think the **robot arm** on line three shows my press is next.
I don't want to learn a new **screen job**.
privateAnswer: Honestly, they've already got a robot arm moving blanks between two presses on line three. It took two blokes off that line. If robots spread even slowly, my press is next, and I don't want to learn some new screen job.

name: Priya Petrov
think: I think robots take the **palletising** first, then the changeovers.
My **changeover skill** is what a machine will copy.
privateAnswer: Privately, the planning and ordering at our plant is probably going to software, and then the robots will come for the palletising first, then the changeovers. I've got a few years. But my thirty-two-minute changeover is exactly the kind of skill a machine will copy.

name: Yusuf Varga
think: I think this is **good for me**, because someone must link software and press.
I already **half do** that job with my spreadsheet.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think it's good for me. The planning office at our plant gets smaller, and someone needs to connect the software to the press. I already half do it with my spreadsheet.

name: Freya Chen
think: I think a **bigger firm** with robots could force the Hollises to follow or close.
Either way there'd be **less work** for me.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'm worried. The Hollis family are good people, but if a bigger carpet firm buys robot creel loaders and halves its costs, the Hollises either follow or close. Either way, there's less for someone like me.

name: Gareth Ibrahim
think: The **office staff** feel it first, and the floor follows when Corbett buys a robot arm.
A robot on the **unload end** means minding two presses, so they'd need half the operators.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, the office gets it first, the planners and the buyers, and we'd see fewer of them. On the floor, Corbett would put a robot arm on the unload end of my press, because that's the easy bit, picking a bracket off a belt. Then I'm minding two presses instead of one, and they need half the operators.

name: Nora Olsen
think: Ordering and **shift planning** move to software first, and office roles aren't replaced.
With a **robot palletiser** and fewer operators per line, I want to be the one setting robots up.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think it's good for me and bad for some of my friends. The ordering and the shift planning go to software first, and Sandra's assistant probably isn't replaced when she leaves. On the floor we'd get a robot palletiser, maybe a robot on the case packer, and fewer operators per line. I want to be the one who sets those robots up, not the one they replace.

name: Victor Torres
think: The **office** will feel this long before my lathes do.
The **robot arms** across the road tell me the floor is next, slowly.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I don't think my lathes get touched for a while. The office will feel it first, the buyers and the scheduling people. But I've seen the robot arms at the plant across the road loading their machines, so I know it's coming for us too, slowly.

name: Daria Baker
think: My **hands-on** job looks safe for a good while yet.
The **paperwork** side of my job, like batch records, would change fast.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I think I'm fine for a good while. The card says robots are slower, and my job's mostly hands-on. But the planning office and quality paperwork would change fast, and some of that paperwork is mine.

name: Emeka Haddad
think: The slow arrival of **robots** gives me years to become the person who fixes them.
The colleagues who **refuse** anything new are the ones at risk.
privateAnswer: Off the record, it's good for me. The office gets hit first, and robots come slowly to the floor, which gives me years to become the person who installs and fixes them. The guys who refuse to touch anything new are the ones I worry about.

name: Lena Novak
think: A **transfer robot** already moves parts between presses on day shift.
More of those means **fewer operators** per line.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'd be watching the presses. We've already got a transfer robot moving parts between press two and three on day shift. If more of those come, they need fewer of us on a line.

name: Tomas Silva
think: I'm OK for a while, but **Ana's** reception job is on the card's list.
If her job shrinks, our **house plan** slows down.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think I'm OK for a while, but Ana's not. She books appointments and answers the phone at a dental practice, which is exactly the list on the card. If her job shrinks, our house plan slows down.

name: Bianca Abbott
think: I'm OK, but Kofi's **testing job** is in the line of fire.
I'd worry for our **household** more than for myself.
privateAnswer: Privately, I'm OK, but Kofi's job is right in the line of fire. Testing software and checking things is the first thing on the card. I'd worry for our household more than for me.

name: Carlos Garcia
think: I'd expect a **robot arm** to load the press once planning goes to software.
Loading is my main task, and it's the part a **robot** does best.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I'd start watching the floor more closely. If the planning goes to software, the next thing the bosses look at is a robot arm loading the press. I'm the guy who loads the press, and loading is the one part a robot does best.

name: Jade Moreau
think: The **batch paperwork**, half an hour a shift, is what software would take.
**Camera checks** would mean fewer operators needed on each shift.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd watch the batch paperwork. Half an hour of every shift is me logging and signing, and that's exactly what software would take. Then the camera checks come in, and the lamp check is my job. I don't think they'd cut me soon, but fewer of us would be needed per shift.

name: Rafael Santos
think: AI helps most with the **thinking side**: programs and job planning.
I'd aim to be the one who **programs and sets up**, not loads.
privateAnswer: Off the record, it means a better job for me. The thinking side of machining, writing the programs and planning the jobs, is where AI helps most, and I already use it. I'd want to be the one who programs the machine and sets it up, not the one who loads the blanks.

name: Zoe Zhang
think: Planning software would tell her which **mould** to change, without knowing the presses.
She fears being the **senior person** who can't read the new screen.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, it reaches me sideways. If the planning goes into software, it's the software telling me which mould to change and when, not Karen (the planner) who knows that press six can't run the thin lids. I've never used any of these AI tools and I don't want to. I'm scared I'll be the senior person who can't read the new screen.

name: Adam Farah
think: Hands-on **setting and measuring** keep his job safe at first.
**Fewer new starters** would make every shift harder.
privateAnswer: For me, honestly, it's probably not bad at first. The program for the lathe might get written by AI, and that's part of my job, but the setting up and measuring is hands. What worries me is fewer new starters, because if there are fewer of us, the shift gets harder.

name: Hana Lopez
think: She's in a **good spot** if she moves now, with robots arriving slowly.
She worries about **Teresa in planning**, who has used spreadsheets for twenty years.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot if I move now. My line is hands-on, so the robots take a while, and I'm already the one who uses the AI tools. The person I worry about is Teresa in the planning office, who's been doing the schedule on a spreadsheet for twenty years.

name: Omar Reyes
think: Nobody's putting AI into a **die change**, so he's safe for a while.
Planning software would **squeeze changeovers**, and robot loaders exist nearby.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think I'm all right for a while, because nobody's putting AI into a die change. But planning tells me what to run, and if a computer does that, it'll squeeze the changeovers harder. And I've seen the robot loaders they put in at the plant in the next valley.

name: Wendy Yilmaz
think: Her **machines** are safe for a good while.
Tom's **warehouse job** is at risk, and her wage alone doesn't cover rent.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think my machines are safe for a good while, but Tom worries me more. His warehouse already has scanners telling him where to walk, and they're talking about robot trolleys. If my partner's warehouse job goes, we're on my wage alone, and my wage doesn't cover the rent.

name: Erik Dubois
think: He's the guy who **speaks both languages**, hands and data.
His worry is Tallis will **expect more** without paying more.
privateAnswer: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The office planning and buying change first, and my job is half hands-on and half watching data. I'm already the guy who speaks both languages. My worry is that Tallis won't pay more for that, just expect it.

name: Fatima Kowalski
think: A **robot arm** already stacks trays in dispatch.
Planning software would **push the line** faster and remove managers who know them.
privateAnswer: Truthfully, I'm not sure the ovens are safe forever. They already have a robot arm stacking trays in the dispatch area. If the planning goes to a computer, it'll push the line faster, and the people upstairs who know us will be gone. That worries me more than I'd say.

name: Marco Quinn
think: AI-planned changes could run the corrugator with **four people**, not six.
His crew would shrink, likely **two of his lads**.
privateAnswer: Privately, I think the corrugator is closer to the edge than people think. The order changes I do by eye are planned by software already, and an AI would make the line run with four people, not six. So my crew shrinks, maybe not me, but two of my lads.

name: Uma Walsh
think: A **helper** or my paid setup hours could be cut.
My **low** pay and thin savings make that a household risk soon.
privateAnswer: I worry management could use faster planning to shorten paid setup time or remove a helper from my shift. With my wage and tiny reserve, a smaller week would hit rent quickly.

name: Colin Costa
think: Software running planning makes **lights-out nights** easier, and nights are my shift.
I'd give it **four or five years** before setters like me are targeted.
privateAnswer: Off the record, slower isn't the same as never. Once the planning and ordering upstairs runs on software, it's easier for them to run the whole plant lights-out on nights, and that's my shift. I'd give it four or five years before they come for setters like me.

name: Dana Jensen
think: My job is mostly **hands-on**, so I'd have some time.
**Planners shrinking** means schedules arrive from software, with fewer people who know the line.
privateAnswer: Off the record, my job is mostly hands-on, so I've got some time. But the planners upstairs will shrink, and then the schedule just lands on my screen from a computer. Fewer people to argue with, fewer people who know the line.

name: Karl Patel
think: Software takes quoting and programming, but someone must make **cells work** together.
That **integration job** is the one I want.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd do well out of this. The quoting and the programming will be done by software, but someone has to make sure the robot cells and the machines actually work together. That's the job I want.

name: Sara Varga
think: Smarter planning means they'll **squeeze the machine** harder.
Our **old plant** might be closed instead of fitted with robots.
privateAnswer: Off the record, the planning office already does our schedule on a screen, and if that gets cleverer they'll squeeze the machine harder. Then the robots come slowly, but our plant is old, and it's cheaper to build a new robot plant than fix ours. That's what scares me.

name: Aaron Bauer
think: I'm fine **for a few years**, but not forever.
Kessler's **welding robots** will lead to robots on our press later.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd think I'm fine for a few years, but that's not forever. Kessler already has two robot arms on the welding line. Once those prove themselves, they'll look at loading our press too.

name: Beth Ibrahim
think: I'm **not worried** about my own job.
My partner Hassan's **IT support** job is exactly what's on the card.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'm not worried for me. I'm worried for my partner Hassan, because IT support is answering questions and fixing logins. That's exactly the stuff on that card.

name: Ivan Okafor
think: The factory down the road already has a **robot loading** its saw.
If it works there, my line could lose **two jobs**.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd watch the factory down the road. They've got a robot loading their saw already. If that works for them, Mr Hollins's son will want one too, and then there's two jobs fewer on my line.

name: Priya Torres
think: My looms are **safe for a while**.
The **order office** will shrink and my shift will be run from a screen.
privateAnswer: Off the record, I'd think my looms are safe for a while, because a robot that ties in threads is a long way off. But the planners and the order office will shrink, and then my shift gets run by a schedule on a screen. I'd want to be the one who understands that screen.

name: Yusuf Alvarez
think: A **lasting** cut could eat my moderate reserve.
**Nearby** posted vacancies are a fallback only if their wage covers my bills.
privateAnswer: The schedule could squeeze changeover hours even if the physical presses still need us. I could cover a short gap with savings, but a lasting cut to my usual wage would use that cushion quickly.

name: Freya Haddad
think: My **senior pay** appears safe while human die work remains.
Rushed **changeovers** could weaken checks even without a lost shift.
privateAnswer: The office could be smaller, and I don't like a rushed changeover, but the physical stamping and die work still need us for now. I don't expect my own senior pay to fall in this slower picture. I worry more about a manager treating a screen as proof that a guard was tested.

name: Gareth Nakamura
think: My own **lead wage** looks safe for now.
A **proven control tool** interests me if it finds thread breaks without adding unpaid work after my shift.
privateAnswer: I expect some change to planning and the office, but the fabric still has to be woven and inspected by us for now. My own pay seems safe. I'd take a proven control tool if it lets me find a thread break without adding an unpaid task at the end of shift.

name: Nora Silva
think: Robot loading could trim the **night premium** I use for household saving.
I might lead the change, but **guarding** and actual paid hours still decide whether it helps.

privateAnswer: My current seal checks will stay for a while, but a capable capper could eventually let fewer operators cover the same output. Nine months saved helps us wait for facts, yet I do not want to lose my higher wage by accepting a vague transfer.

name: Aaron Quinn
think: A **robot** may eventually reduce press hours despite my setting skill.
A **year** saved gives time but does not replace my higher wage.
privateAnswer: My setting knowledge stays useful now, but a robot taking blanks in and parts out could reduce operator hours later. A year saved lets me wait for evidence; it does not mean I want a smaller lead wage.

name: Beth Walsh
think: One lead could cover **two forming cells**, cutting my hours.
New robots may remove **routine bottle checks** first.
privateAnswer: A vision system may take routine bottle checks, and a robot stacker may later reduce the crew. I could keep a lead role but might lose paid shifts if two forming cells are put under one lead.

name: Ivan Costa
think: Physical arms may remove **helper shifts**.
My **lead wage** looks steady, though the new line changes the crew.
privateAnswer: A faster schedule might change orders first, then a robot arm could lift tyres from the mould. I think my lead job would hold for now, but two helpers might lose shifts, and I would want their names in the staffing plan.

name: Priya Jensen
think: My **lead hours** could shrink if one operator covers two cutters.
Arun's wage and our **strong reserve** give time, but do not make a cut harmless.
privateAnswer: I might lose some lead hours if one person is made to cover two cutters after the new camera arrives. Arun's heating wage and our savings help, but I do not want to burn that cushion because someone calls a smaller roster efficient. I would wait for a working line before trusting the sales figures.

name: Yusuf Patel
think: My **setup hours** could shrink under a two-line roster.
Fourteen months saved and **Leena's shop** help, but neither guarantees equal future wages.
privateAnswer: I can learn a new screen quickly, but the factory might use it to trim my paid setup hours. Leena's shop helps, yet the customer work is not a regular second high wage. My fourteen-month reserve gives me choices, not a reason to let our base pay slip quietly.

name: Freya Varga
think: A short **folder shift** could be lost while I am still learning.
Our **thin reserve** and variable cleaning pay cannot bridge rent easily.
privateAnswer: I am still the learner on the folder, and a new schedule might take away one of my short paid shifts. My partner's office cleaning is already irregular. With less than a month saved, a lost shift would go straight through our rent budget.

name: Gareth Bauer
think: A cut to **paid hours** would hurt a household already short of reserve.
Occasional checked AI explanations are useful, but **hands-on qualification** needs supervised press time.
privateAnswer: A new screen could take some checking work from our shift. The concern is whether the plant cuts paid hours while I still have rent and my wife has only part-time wages. I could learn a better changeover method if the place and paid time are real.

name: Nora Ibrahim
think: A **later** automatic feeder could cut the newest operators first.
Our **savings** will not cover a lasting reduction in hours.
privateAnswer: I can learn a new screen quickly, but I am still junior on the physical sealer. If an automatic tray feeder later takes a whole station, the newest workers may lose hours first. Our tiny savings would not cover a long cut.

name: Victor Okafor
think: A **later** automatic loader may reduce my junior fabric-cutting shifts.
**Three** weeks saved cannot cover a long job search.
privateAnswer: I can still see a crooked fabric edge, but an automatic loader could let fewer people work a shift. As a newer cutter, I would be near the front of any hours cut. Three weeks saved would go before I found another local job.

name: Daria Torres
think: My **junior label checks** may disappear as the camera takes more of the routine work.
Mateo’s **grocery shifts** cannot cover our bills without my wage.
privateAnswer: The camera might take label checks I am still learning, and I could be one of the first juniors to lose hours. Mateo’s grocery pay cannot cover our bills alone, and nearby packaging jobs are scarce.

name: Emeka Alvarez
think: A camera may remove **my simple glaze checks** before I have mastered the whole line.
Leena’s **porter pay** cannot cover our housing fee alone.
privateAnswer: A camera could take the simple glaze checks I do now. I learn tools quickly, but I have the least experience on this crew; if a shift disappears, Leena’s porter pay cannot cover our housing fee alone.

name: Lena Haddad
think: My **junior shift** could disappear if changeovers are shortened.
Karim's **variable guard pay** and two weeks saved cannot replace it.
privateAnswer: If the office shortens our changeover time, my junior shift could be the easiest to drop. Karim's guard rota cannot promise the difference, and two weeks saved is not enough for one missed wage. I am not ready to learn from a screen by myself.

name: Tomas Nakamura
think: My **test shift** could shrink if a camera changes the coiling roster.
Akiko's bakery wage and our **three-week reserve** cannot fill a lost factory week.
privateAnswer: If a camera starts measuring springs, my test work might be folded into one other operator's shift. My low wage is still needed for rent and heating, and Akiko's bakery hours can change. Three weeks saved makes even one lost week serious.

name: Bianca Silva
think: Shorter runs could cut **paid hours** before robot capping arrives.
My husband’s **bike-shop pay** cannot reliably replace a lost line shift.
privateAnswer: I'm quick to try a tool, but I am not yet quick at changeovers. If office planning moves to software, the line could get shorter runs and fewer paid hours. That would reach our rent before any robot touched a bottle.

name: Carlos Ziegler
think: Junior **changeover hours** could shrink and use up our reserve.
I trust **hands-on instruction** more than an unchecked AI answer about a hot press.
privateAnswer: A computer could shorten production runs, and juniors may be first to lose paid changeover hours. Three months of savings would give us time, but it would not replace a wage indefinitely. I don't want to learn the plant through AI answers I cannot check.

name: Jade Garcia
think: A **later** robot feeder may cut my junior gasket-line shifts.
**Four** months saved cannot replace a lasting wage cut.
privateAnswer: A robot feeder could remove a helper and later leave fewer shifts for someone still junior like me. Four months saved would buy time but not restore a cut wage. Nina’s care visits have variable hours, so I would want exact figures.

name: Rafael Mensah
think: A **later** coil-loading robot may cut my junior winding hours.
**Three** months saved cannot carry a long rent gap.
privateAnswer: A robot loader might cut packing and operator hours later; I am still new enough to be exposed. Three months saved will not carry many months of rent. I can pick up a new interface quickly, but only a real shift plan shows whether that helps me.

name: Zoe Santos
think: My **junior pattern checks** may be removed first if cameras take the simple fabric checks.
Sal’s **bakery wage** cannot replace my paid shift alone.
privateAnswer: The camera could take the simple pattern checks I am still learning. I might lose a paid shift before an experienced cutter does, and Sal’s bakery counter wage would not cover the mortgage and both our bills alone.

name: Adam Young
think: My **junior checking hours** could be reduced by a camera.
Fran’s **shop wage** cannot meet our rent alone.
privateAnswer: The camera could judge the simple bare corners I spot now, and a robot might load the hooks. I am still the junior operator, so my paid week could shrink; Fran’s shop wage alone would not cover our rent and bills.

name: Hana Farah
think: My **junior hours** could shrink if one operator watches two drums.
Four months saved and **Farid's wage** help, but do not replace my rent money.
privateAnswer: I am still junior on the roaster, so one person watching two drums could make my hours shrink. Four months saved and Farid's porter pay give us time, but my wage matters for the rent. I am willing to learn the camera if its mistakes are shown, not hidden.

name: Omar Larsen
think: My **newer filler shift** could shrink under a two-machine roster.
Marta's wage and **three months saved** cannot replace my regular pay indefinitely.
privateAnswer: One operator might be asked to watch two fillers if a new system counts jars and finds crooked wicks. I am the newer person on this machine, so my hours could be the ones to shrink. Marta's classroom wage and three months saved would not replace a whole factory week for long.

name: Wendy Reyes
think: A **later** roll-loading robot could cut my junior label-press shifts.
**Five** months saved cannot carry a long wage cut.
privateAnswer: A robot loader could eventually leave fewer people tending the label press. I am still junior and would be easier to replace than the senior printer. Five months saved helps us wait, but it cannot cover a long cut to my wage.

name: Erik Weber
think: A **later** loader could cut junior router shifts.
**Nearly** four months saved cannot carry a long wage gap.
privateAnswer: A loader could eventually let fewer operators cover the router. I am still junior, so I would be easy to leave off a shift. Nearly four months saved helps, but it cannot replace my ordinary wage for long.

name: Fatima Dubois
think: Shorter runs could remove my **evening premium** or paid hours.
The **ten-month reserve** gives me options, but another plant may pay less.
privateAnswer: I don't use AI and don't want a screen telling me to reach into a moving loom. Planning changes could shorten our runs and threaten my evening premium. Ten months saved gives me time to object or look at another textile plant, but I prefer to keep the good shift if I can.

name: Marco Khan
think: Shorter runs could reduce my **late premium** before retirement is funded.
I can learn a **proven screen**, but a hot machine still needs a lead operator.
privateAnswer: Planning changes could mean shorter runs and fewer late shifts. Our reserve would cushion that, but I would not want to lose the premium just as we are trying to settle the retirement numbers. I can learn a proven display; I cannot learn a hot sealer safely from a chat box.

name: Uma Quinn
think: A camera could remove **my junior checks**.
My **night shifts** may be the first cut despite a strong reserve.
privateAnswer: The camera could take the simple thickness checks I am still learning. I use AI daily and could learn a new station, but being a junior on nights means my own hours could be cut first.

name: Colin Wagner
think: My **junior weekend hours** could be cut first if a stacker takes the simple work.
Rina’s **shop pay** cannot carry the housing loan alone.
privateAnswer: A camera could check simple curls while a stacker takes the pallet job. I am still junior on the press, so one of my weekend shifts could go first; Rina’s hardware-shop pay alone would not cover our housing loan and bills.

name: Dana Costa
think: A smaller **night roster** could cut my higher wage even while the divider runs.
Ten months saved and **Leon’s pay** give time, not a replacement for lost premium.
privateAnswer: The divider still needs hands, but software might spread the same work across fewer night shifts and take away the premium I rely on. Leon's pay and ten months saved help, yet a lower rate would change our monthly sums. I am open to a new camera after someone else proves it catches a light biscuit.

name: Karl Ito
think: Merged late shifts could take away my **above-usual pay**.
Fourteen months **saved** buys time but cannot restore a permanently lower rate.
privateAnswer: I like new tools, but a tidy plan could let the plant merge late shifts and take away the rate that makes my pay high. We could absorb a short spell from savings and Mei's wage, but I would not call a permanent lower rate harmless. My daily AI manual searches are no substitute for learning a new brake control properly.

name: Sara Patel
think: My **night premium** could shrink with shorter runs.
Our **eight-month reserve** gives time, but nearby jobs may pay less.
privateAnswer: Shorter runs could take away some of my night premium. We could manage for a while with savings and my husband's van wage, but I would miss a good pay rate. Plenty of nearby plants does not mean every one has the same safe night shift.

name: Aaron Usman
think: A shorter batch could remove **weekend premium** pay.
Our **reserve and local jobs** give options, but a new plant may pay less.
privateAnswer: Software might shorten batches and take a weekend from my rota. Our reserve and nearby plants mean we have options, but I would rather keep the premium while I can. I use AI occasionally at home, yet that does not qualify me to set a cable winder.

name: Beth Bauer
think: A camera may remove **my simple fill checks**.
Being **junior on nights** leaves my own paid hours exposed.
privateAnswer: A camera might take the easy fill checks I do now, and a loader might later take another pair of hands. I am still junior on this line, so my own hours could be cut even with strong savings.

name: Ivan Hansen
think: Faster targets and a robot stacker could cut **my paid hours** on the gluer.
Few **nearby plants** leave little room for a bad offer after bus fares.
privateAnswer: The first change might be software setting faster targets, then a robot stacker could take the second operator’s hours. We barely cover rent as it is, and there is no line of similar plants down the road.

name: Priya Okafor
think: One lost **paid shift** would strain bills on our lower wage.
A thin **cash reserve** gives little time to find another local job.
privateAnswer: A camera might make the line easier, but management could use it to run with one fewer operator. On our low pay, losing a shift would mean missing a bill; there is hardly a reserve behind us. I would try a proven display on a paid supervised shift, not a sales pitch.

name: Yusuf Tanaka
think: A merged **short-shift roster** could cut an already low wage.
Rina's **irregular catering** cannot reliably cover missing hours.
privateAnswer: I like testing things. A tighter schedule can turn two short shifts into one and cut my already low wages. Rina cannot promise catering hours to fill that gap. The camera might catch a crooked print, but it must not become an excuse to remove the spotter without proving it safe.

name: Freya Alvarez
think: **Robot** spraying may later cut my paid conveyor-operator shifts.
**Two** weeks saved and few nearby jobs leave little margin.
privateAnswer: A spray arm could make fewer operators necessary later even if I still know the oven well. Two weeks saved would disappear with one short rota. I cannot rely on another coating vacancy nearby.

name: Gareth Gupta
think: A **robot** may cut moulding shifts even for experienced operators.
**Three** weeks saved and few local jobs mean little search time.
privateAnswer: A robot unloader could leave fewer people on the moulding shift later. I am experienced but not the specialist they would retain first. Three weeks saved would not buy much job-search time, and local openings are scarce.

name: Nora Nakamura
think: Combined batches could cut **setup hours** and threaten rent quickly.
I can learn an **approved alarm log**, but it must match the paper chart.
privateAnswer: Canning is physical, but a smarter schedule could combine batches and remove my paid setup hours. With less than a month saved, even a small cut would hit rent. I can learn a useful new display quickly if I am allowed to practise on a real paid shift.

name: Victor Schmidt
think: Shorter runs could cut **my setup pay** soon.
A **thin reserve** leaves little room for missed days, even with my experience.
privateAnswer: A new order plan might make shorter runs, and my setup hours could go. With less than a month saved, I cannot shrug off even a few missing days. I do not use AI and would only learn a new machine routine if the teaching is paid and someone stands beside me.

name: Daria Ziegler
think: A **later** robot may cut tufting hours despite my experience.
**Three** weeks saved and scarce textile jobs leave little room.
privateAnswer: If a robot threads and clears the machine, the floor may need fewer hands even though I know the pile checks. Our three weeks saved cannot carry a long hours cut. There are few similar jobs nearby.

name: Emeka Fischer
think: A **later** loader may cut my press hours.
A **quick** new screen skill cannot replace a lost wage.
privateAnswer: A loader could eventually take hands off the mould line, including some of my hours. I am quick with a new screen, but that will not keep a position open if the roster shrinks. Less than three weeks saved gives us little time to find other work.

name: Lena Mensah
think: The **tins I inspect** could be pulled by a later robot.
A **four-month cushion** would not replace a long wage cut.
privateAnswer: A robot might eventually pull the tins I inspect and take a few hours from our crew. Kojo’s bus route still pays, but four months saved would not cover a long cut to my own pay.

name: Tomas Rossi
think: Robot packing could reduce **my paid shifts** on the extrusion line.
Some **nearby openings** may help, but net wages after travel still matter.
privateAnswer: I can imagine fewer people on the packing end once robots spread, though extrusion itself still needs watching. Losing even a few paid shifts would press our loan, and the other nearby plants have only some openings.

name: Bianca Young
think: Merged **paid shifts** could reduce my ordinary operator wage.
Elise's pay and four months **saved** allow only limited adjustment.
privateAnswer: I am curious about the camera, yet management might join shifts if it reduces scrap and take away some of my ordinary wage. Elise's steady dispatcher pay and four months saved give us a little room, not an open-ended replacement. The test must prove it sees a wandering edge before anyone removes the catcher.

name: Carlos Evans
think: A shorter **paid roster** could cut the household income.
Three months **saved** and June's wage cannot replace long-term lost shifts.
privateAnswer: I am wary of an AI screen on the kiln; I have never used one, and I would not accept a shorter roster on a salesperson's promise. Three months saved could absorb a small interruption, but lost shifts would cut our household income. June's library wage covers part of our costs, not all of them.
